content: The 2006 North American E. coli outbreak occurred in two distinct phases and involved the foodborne pathogen Escherichia coli O157:H7, a bacterium capable of causing severe illness, including bloody diarrhea and dehydration. The first phase of the outbreak, which began in September 2006, was linked to fresh spinach, while the second phase, occurring in November and December 2006, was initially attributed to green onions but later determined to be caused by prepackaged iceberg lettuce. In total, at least 276 cases of illness were reported, though no deaths were associated with the second phase. First Outbreak: Spinach (September 2006) In September 2006, an outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 infections was traced to fresh spinach in 26 U.S. states. By October 6, 2006, 199 individuals had been infected, with three fatalities and 31 cases of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a severe complication involving kidney failure. The strain of E. coli involved in this outbreak was particularly virulent, with hospitalization rates reaching 50%, significantly higher than the 25-30% typically seen in past outbreaks. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a nationwide warning advising consumers to avoid all fresh spinach and spinach-containing products. The agency also noted that washing the spinach was unlikely to remove the bacteria, as it was hypothesized that the contamination might be systemic, meaning the bacteria could have been absorbed into the plant through its roots. However, this theory was later deemed unproven. The source of the outbreak was identified as organic bagged spinach grown on a 50-acre farm in San Benito County, California. Investigations by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the California Department of Health Services (CDHS) suggested that the contamination likely originated from irrigation water tainted with cattle feces or from grazing deer. Further analysis implicated Paicines Ranch, an Angus cattle ranch that had leased land to Mission Organics, the spinach grower. E. coli O157:H7 matching the outbreak strain was found in water and cattle manure samples collected from the ranch, some of which were located within a mile of the spinach fields. Additional environmental risk factors included the presence of wild pigs and the proximity of surface waterways to irrigation wells. Flaws in the transportation and processing systems of the spinach producer may have exacerbated the spread of contamination. In response to the outbreak, California's agricultural industry implemented voluntary good agricultural practices to mitigate the risk of E. coli contamination in leafy greens. Two companies, Natural Selection Foods LLC and River Ranch Fresh Foods, issued recalls of spinach and spinach-containing products. Natural Selection Foods, which marketed spinach under multiple brand names, announced that its organic produce had been cleared of contamination by an independent agency but maintained its recall as a precaution. A third company, RLB Food Distributors, later recalled spinach-containing salad products in several East Coast states. Impact of the First Outbreak The spinach-related outbreak affected 26 states, with at least 200 confirmed cases of illness as of December 23, 2006. Three deaths were directly linked to the outbreak: an elderly woman in Wisconsin, a two-year-old child in Idaho, and an elderly woman in Nebraska. A fourth death in Maryland remained under investigation. The outbreak also extended to Canada, where one case was reported. The economic impact on California, which produces 75% of the nation's spinach, was significant, with estimated losses of up to $74 million. The spinach crop in California was valued at $258.3 million in 2005, and each acre lost represented approximately $3,500 in revenue. Timeline of the First Outbreak September 14, 2006: The FDA issued a warning about E. coli contamination in bagged spinach, advising consumers to avoid the product. September 17, 2006: The warning was expanded to include all fresh spinach and spinach-containing products. September 18, 2006: Illinois and Nebraska reported their first cases, bringing the total number of affected states to 21. The death of a two-year-old in Ohio was under investigation. September 20, 2006: The CDC confirmed that the genetic fingerprint of E. coli O157:H7 found in a package of Dole Baby Spinach matched the outbreak strain. September 29, 2006: The FDA narrowed its warning to specific brands and packaging dates. October 5, 2006: The FBI launched a criminal investigation into the outbreak. October 26, 2006: The final toll of the spinach outbreak included 199 infections across 28 states, 141 hospitalizations, 31 cases of kidney failure, and three deaths. Second Outbreak: Lettuce (November-December 2006) In December 2006, an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak was linked to Taco Bell restaurants in four Northeastern states. A total of 71 individuals fell ill, with 52 confirmed cases of the outbreak strain. The affected states included New Jersey (33 cases), New York (22 cases), Pennsylvania (13 cases), Delaware (2 cases), and South Carolina (1 case, linked to a Taco Bell in Pennsylvania). Of those affected, 53 were hospitalized, and eight developed HUS. Initial investigations pointed to green onions as the source, but further analysis implicated prepackaged iceberg lettuce supplied by Ready Pac, a produce processing company. The contaminated lettuce was traced to farms in California's Central Valley, though specific sources were not disclosed. A separate outbreak in December 2006 was linked to Taco John's restaurants in Iowa and Minnesota. At least 50 cases were reported in Iowa, and 37 probable cases were identified in Minnesota. Nine individuals were confirmed to have E. coli infections, eight were hospitalized, and one developed HUS. The source of the contamination was traced to lettuce supplied by a Minneapolis-based distributor. Taco John's responded by reimbursing affected individuals for medical expenses and switching to a new produce supplier. Regulatory and Industry Response The 2006 outbreaks prompted legislative proposals at both state and federal levels to strengthen food safety regulations.
